title: Traffic Rules, Accidents and Challans (Traffic Fines)
summary: Which papers to keep with you, the road rules, what to do after an accident, and how to check and pay a real challan (a traffic fine ticket).
keyPoints: Keep a valid driving licence, RC, insurance and PUC; digital copies in DigiLocker are accepted.
After an accident, stop, help the injured, call 108 or 112, and tell the police if there is injury.
Check any challan on the official e-Challan website; never pay through a link in an SMS.
Never drive after drinking alcohol; the legal limit is a Blood Alcohol Concentration of 0.03%.
Wear a helmet on a two-wheeler and a seat belt in a car, including the rear seat.

body.text: On the road, drivers and traffic police both have clear duties. If you know them, you can avoid arguments. You can also avoid paying a fine you do not owe.
📄 Papers you must keep with you

items: A valid driving licence (a licence that has not expired) for the type of vehicle you drive.

Registration certificate (RC) (the paper that shows the vehicle is registered in your name), insurance, and pollution under control (PUC) certificate (proof that your vehicle's smoke is within the allowed limit).
If it is a commercial vehicle (one used to earn money, like a taxi or a goods vehicle), a permit and a fitness certificate.

body.text: Digital copies (copies on your phone) in DigiLocker or the mParivahan app are accepted by law as valid papers during a traffic check.

items: Follow signals and road signs. Stop at red, go at green, and never block a junction (a place where roads meet).
Do not cross the speed limit set for the road. Slow down near schools, hospitals and pedestrian crossings.
Never drive on the wrong side. Never overtake (go past another vehicle) from the left.
Do not use a mobile phone while driving. Use a hands-free device only where it is safe and allowed by law.
Wear a helmet (head cover) on a two-wheeler. Wear a seat belt in a car, including in the rear seat.
Never drive after drinking alcohol; it is illegal. The legal limit is a Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) of 0.03% (30 mg per 100 ml of blood).
Stop at once. Switch on the hazard lights. Help anyone who is hurt. Call 108 or 112.
If there is injury, death or serious damage, tell the police. Leaving the spot is a serious offence (a crime).
Exchange names, phone numbers, vehicle numbers and insurer details with the other driver.
Note the time and place. Take photos if you can. Also check if there is a CCTV (security camera) nearby.
Tell your insurance company within the time your policy allows, and get a copy of the accident report.

body.text: 🧾 Challan (traffic fine ticket): check before you pay

items: Check the challan on the official e-Challan website using the challan number or your vehicle number.
Never pay through a link in an SMS. Real payments happen only on the official website or at the police station.
If you think it is wrong, you can pay online, or argue against it in the court set up for this.
Always keep the receipt until the matter is closed.

body.text: Never hand over your original documents and walk away. Show them, but do not give up the originals unless there is a legal reason and you get a receipt.
A police officer cannot take away your vehicle or keys for a routine paper check. They can take it only for certain offences listed in the law, and then you must get a receipt.

items: Traffic rules are standard legal guidelines. They keep people safe, control the flow of vehicles, and protect pedestrians (people walking on the road).
In India, these rules come mainly from the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

body.text: 👣 Which side to drive on and how to overtake

items: Keep to the LEFT. Oncoming traffic (vehicles coming towards you) passes on your right.
Overtake (go past another vehicle) only from the RIGHT, and only after signalling.
Never overtake on bends, hills or bridges.
Obey the posted speed limit (the maximum speed allowed on that road).
Slow down to about 25 km/h near schools, road workers and public processions.

body.text: 🚦 Traffic signals: what each colour means

items: RED: stop completely.
YELLOW: slow down safely.
GREEN: you may go.

body.text: 🪖 Safety rules for seat belts, helmets and phones

items: Seat belts are mandatory for all occupants (everyone travelling in the car).
Helmets are compulsory for both the rider and the pillion (the person sitting behind the rider).
Do not use a mobile phone or any hand-held device while driving.
Give free passage to ambulances and fire vehicles.
Pedestrians have the right of way at zebra crossings (the white stripes where people cross the road).

body.text: 🧾 Fines under the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019

items: Driving without a licence: about Rs 5,000.
Drunk driving: about Rs 10,000 and/or up to 6 months in jail.
Riding without a helmet: about Rs 1,000 plus a 3-month licence disqualification.
Not wearing a seat belt: about Rs 1,000.
Over-speeding: about Rs 1,000 to Rs 2,000 for a light motor vehicle.

practicalSteps: Keep digital copies of RC, licence, insurance and PUC in DigiLocker.
Note down the challan number, date, place and the officer's details.
Check and pay on the official e-Challan website, or argue against it in court within the time allowed.
After any accident, save 108/112, tell your insurer, and keep the photos and the accident report.
exceptions: In some states, some papers can be shown later at the police station or online, within a fixed time.
The helmet and seat-belt rules have a few exceptions. For example, some medical conditions, if you can show proof.

faqs.q: Can the police take away my vehicle keys?
faqs.a: There is no general power to take your keys or your vehicle for a routine paper check. They can take it only for certain offences listed in the law, and then you must get a receipt.

faqs.q: Is a copy of my documents enough?
faqs.a: Digital copies through DigiLocker or mParivahan are accepted. Otherwise carry the originals or certified copies.

sources.label: Parivahan Sewa (Ministry of Road Transport and Highways)

misconceptions.myth: Traffic police can always take my licence on the spot.
misconceptions.fact: For many paper offences, the law lets you show the papers later. Taking them away at once is allowed only in certain situations.
